RX e angio-TC del torace senza polmonite: Chest X-ray and CT angiogram without pneumonia in a COVID-19-positive patient; CT angiogram with insufficient opacification of the pulmonary arteries
Donna di 22 anni, in gravidanza, obesa (: 22-year-old pregnant woman, obese (BMI about 52), swab positive for SARS-CoV-2, dyspnea. Bedside chest X-ray the day before; today chest CT angiogram for suspected pulmonary embolism.
Referta in ordine: RX, angio-TC, conclus: Report in order: X-ray, CT angiogram, conclusion.
Saper riconoscere un esame negativo è im:
Recognizing a negative exam is as important as finding an abnormality. A positive swab does not mean pneumonia: in the early stages, or in mild forms, CT may be normal.
In a CT angiogram for embolism ALWAYS check quality first (here insufficient: the bolus arrived early, contrast is still in the superior vena cava and the pulmonary arteries are poorly opacified): opacification of the pulmonary arteries (at least 250 HU in the trunk), motion and contrast artifacts (mixed flow from the inferior vena cava, common in pregnancy due to increased cardiac output), then the branches down to the segmental level.
In pregnancy the choice between perfusion scintigraphy and CT angiogram depends on the X-ray and on availability; the uterine dose of CT angiogram is very low, the breast dose higher. Severe obesity reduces the quality of X-ray and CT (noise, low volumes).
Prima di dire «niente embolia» misura l': Before saying "no embolism", measure the opacification of the pulmonary trunk: below 250 HU the study does not exclude peripheral emboli.
Tampone positivo per SARS-CoV-2; nessun: Swab positive for SARS-CoV-2; no intensive care unit admission (COVID-19-AR clinical data). Original reports: X-ray "No pleural effusion, pneumothorax or consolidation"; CT angiogram "No focal airspace opacification or pleural effusion, no significant evidence of pulmonary vascular congestion".
Donna in gravidanza con dispnea: l'angio: Pregnant woman with dyspnea: the CT angiogram is non-diagnostic (insufficient opacification of the pulmonary arteries), so embolism is NOT excluded. The physician treating the patient should be notified verbally shortly, so that an alternative exam (for example repeating with a correct bolus or perfusion scintigraphy) or treatment can be decided; writing it only in the report risks "no pneumonia" being read as a negative exam.
